reasoning: The mmap is real. ClaudeSessionScanner.swift:91 and CodexSessionScanner.swift:128 map the files with Data(contentsOf:options:[.mappedIfSafe]), so a file that shrinks mid-scan can in theory raise SIGBUS. The claimed damage does not hold up, though. The only source is write access to ~/.claude/projects or ~/.codex/sessions, which means code already running as the same user in the same single-user desktop session. That code can already kill the process directly (kill -9), delete or corrupt the config, read the same credentials, or stop the app from launching. Crashing the menu-bar app through a truncation race gives it nothing it did not already have: no privilege or trust boundary is crossed, and the finding itself says nothing is disclosed. It also cannot hurt integrity. A short read or crash cannot write to disk or change credentials, and the memo or cache just gets rebuilt on the next launch. A legitimate writer (the Claude or Codex CLI) only appends to these transcripts, and appending does not cause SIGBUS. Only shrinking a file does, so accidental real-world triggering is unlikely. The result is a robustness or hardening issue (a plain read would remove the SIGBUS window), not a security impact. The same pattern appears at UsageHistoryStore.swift:95 and 142 on app-owned files, with the same conclusion.
